$comment: Every number this page draws, tied to the committed blob it came from.
The page's thesis is 'every number is traceable to the repository it came
from'. Until this file existed that was a slogan: the plates and the prose
were checked against EACH OTHER (gate.mjs check 9) and against nothing else,
so two authored strings could agree perfectly and both be false. Three rounds
of audits found exactly that.
A row is a derivation, not a citation. `extractor` is a shell command run
against $BLOB — the file fetched from raw.githubusercontent.com at `ref`,
which is a COMMIT SHA, never a branch name. Its stdout must equal `value`
exactly. Nobody has to trust the number; they run the command.
`drawn_on` is where the value appears on this page. build/claims.mjs checks
both directions: every row must re-derive, AND every number a plate draws
must have a row here or an entry in `exempt`. A claims file that only
verified the numbers it happened to list would be the same gate-that-cannot-
fail this project has already shipped twice.

applied-web.note: The in-browser ONNX build is NOT on main. The commit is pushed and public, so it pins and re-derives like any other — but the page must say which branch it is reading, and does.

claims.note: Counted from the error list itself, not from 10000-9701 — so the 299 marks the plate draws and the number beside them come from one artifact.
Column 4 is pred_activation — the softmax mass on the label it wrongly chose.
Derived from the two scores, not stored — so it cannot drift from them.
The row the page keeps because it loses to it.
The dispatch table itself, not the import list — the import list agrees at 36, but routes are what the function actually serves.
Vercel's Hobby-tier limit is a platform fact, not a repo fact. What the repo can prove is that this limit is the reason the dispatcher exists, which is what the page claims.
This is the row that keeps the hero honest: the artifact itself says the score was produced with the rules layer alone, which is what the plate labels it.

claims.extractor: python3 -c "import ast,sys;t=ast.parse(open(sys.argv[1]).read());print(sum(1 for n in ast.walk(t) if isinstance(n,ast.AnnAssign) and getattr(n.target,'id','')=='PATTERNS' for s in ast.walk(n.value) if isinstance(s,ast.Constant) and isinstance(s.value,str)))" "$BLOB"
claims.note: Parsed, not grepped. A second method — counting r-string lines inside the PATTERNS block — also gives 201.
The build really does fail below this: it is a CI flag, not a doc sentence.
The byte length of the committed artifact, read from the contents API at that SHA. Not on main — see the applied-web repo entry.

One annotation per fixed vulnerability, in the docstring of the method that carried it: attachments 1, calendars 1, events 2 (read + delete), tags 1, task-lists 1, tasks 2 (read + delete). The commit log agrees by a second method — six `fix(security): scope …` commits, four of which name two methods.

claims.drawn_as: plate-2-jetpack.svg draws it one hex glyph per <text>, twice — the vectorised row and the java.util.zip row — so the string never appears whole in the extracted text. The per-glyph digits are exempted below and point back at this row.
claims.note: The canonical Adler-32 vector for the input "Wikipedia", asserted for both the scalar and the vectorised path (Adler32Test.java:36-37). The stronger claim on the plate — bit-identical to java.util.zip — is the separate matchesJdkAcrossSizes test, which compares both paths against java.util.zip.Adler32 across 26 input sizes.

unpinnable.why: github.com/yadava5/ai-augmented-auto-ml-toolchain is PRIVATE, so raw.githubusercontent.com serves nothing to an anonymous reader and no extractor here can be run by anyone but its owner. It is drawn as a 64px hero — the largest unverifiable number on the page.
unpinnable.options: make the repo public, replace the hero with a claim the reader can check, or state on the plate that this one is not publicly derivable.

$comment: Numbers a plate draws that are not measurements of a repository — names,
versions, viewBox geometry, and the glyphs of a hex constant. Each needs a
reason. Prefer a file-scoped key ('plate-2-jetpack.svg:6') over a bare one:
a global exemption for '6' would wave through an unsourced 6 anywhere in
the document. claims.mjs also fails on an exemption no plate uses, so this
list cannot quietly accumulate excuses for numbers that are already gone.
